analysis.one_liner: Bars brand-generic deals that delay cheaper generic drugs from reaching the market.
analysis.headline: The bill, meant to speed cheaper generic drugs to market, died in committee with zero cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the first generic company to file for FDA approval of a copy of a brand-name drug gets 180 days of exclusive sales. Some brand and generic companies strike deals where the generic agrees to hold off on launching until after that exclusivity window expires, keeping cheaper copies off the market even longer. This bill would strip first-in-line status from generic companies that sign such launch-delay agreements, let the next generic in line take their place, and require the companies to file the text of these agreements with the FDA within ten business days.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs with no generic alternative would get cheaper generic versions sooner, because the deals that park the first generic's exclusivity would no longer block other generic makers from stepping in. Other generic drug manufacturers would gain earlier access to markets that are currently locked up, and insurers, employers, and Medicare would pay less when generics arrive faster.

how_it_helps.text: The bill disqualifies a generic applicant from the valuable 180-day first-filer exclusivity if it has agreed with the brand-name maker or a patent holder not to seek approval or start selling until another applicant's exclusivity period expires [S2].

It expands who counts as a 'first applicant' so that a back-up generic company — one that filed after the first day but has no patent suit against it — can qualify for the 180-day exclusivity if the first filer struck a launch-delay deal or was blocked in court [S2, S3].
It requires brand and generic companies to submit the text, or a full written description, of any agreement to defer a generic's approval or launch to the FDA within 10 business days of signing [S3].

If an agreement sets several possible launch dates, the bill forces the generic to use the earliest date in the deal, or launch within 180 days of another first applicant selling — closing a way to stretch the delay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose the extra months or years of monopoly pricing that launch-delay settlements buy them. Generic companies that profit by agreeing to park their 180-day exclusivity would lose that revenue stream. Patent holders would also face a tighter window to sue a generic applicant for infringement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and settling generic firms

drawbacks.text: The launch-delay agreements filed with the FDA would be exempt from public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act — only Congress or parties to an administrative or judicial proceeding could see them — so the public would not be able to examine the deals the bill targets [S3].

The bill limits patent holders to a single infringement suit within the standard 45-day window, so a patent owner whose legitimate patent is challenged would lose the ability to sue a later generic applicant who enters the market [S3].
The bill is narrow: it applies only to drugs in the 180-day exclusivity program and only to agreements signed after enactment, so delay tactics outside that regime would be untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in scope: it closes a specific loophole — deals that park a first generic's 180-day exclusivity — rather than banning all pay-for-delay settlements, and it applies only going forward. The costs fall on brand drug makers' extended monopoly profits and on settling generic firms, which is the point of the bill. The main design flaws are the secrecy of the FDA filings and the tighter patent-suit window, both of which an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to subcommittees in the spring of 2019, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nanette Diaz Barragan introduced the FAIR Generics Act on March 5, 2019, with no cosponsors [S1, S4, S5].

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, then split to the Health Subcommittee and the Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet Subcommittee within a month [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill sat in subcommittee with zero cosponsors until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: the settlements that delay generic competitors stayed legal and unexamined, and patients kept paying brand-name prices for longer than they otherwise might have.

sides.party_line_note: No party bloc ever took a position: the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a floor vote [S4].

industries.note: Brand companies use settlements in which a generic agrees to stay off the market until another applicant's 180-day exclusivity runs out, extending monopoly pricing. The bill would disqualify generics that sign such deals and force disclosure of the agreements to the FDA, cutting off that revenue-extension tool [S2, S3].

Generic firms that monetize launch-delay deals would lose that income, but other generic makers would gain earlier access to markets now locked up, because back-up applicants could qualify for first-filer exclusivity [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Faster generic entry lowers drug costs, which flows to insurers, employers, and public programs that pay drug claims [S2].
